未来纳指有望连续跑赢标普
这轮加息周期里，资金正在从全面撒网转向极度集中，而这种集中的方向，跟1999年那轮加息周期的走法非常像。

过去大家习惯的逻辑是市场好的时候资金会比较均匀地流向各个板块，等权重指数(RSP)、小盘股(IWM)这类代表市场广度的标的会跟着一起走强。最近RSP和IWM的结构偏弱，说明主力资金不愿意雨露均沾了。

取而代之的是一种更极端的集中打法，所有的资本被挤压进一条极窄的通道，只往那些对利率不敏感、同时资本回报率(ROIC)极高的公司里砸。

为什么会这样？因为像Meta、Amazon、Google这些巨头手里握着百亿级的充沛现金流，多加25个基点的借贷成本对它们来说根本不痛不痒，它们庞大的AI资本开支不会因为加息放缓。加息对这批现金流极强的公司没有杀伤力，但对那些依赖借贷扩张、现金流本来就紧张的中小盘公司，压力就完全不一样了。这也是为什么资金会往头部集中。

这个走势，跟1999年那轮加息周期非常像。

历史上1999年美联储开启连续加息的时候，发生过一件挺反直觉的事。标普500当时表现相当平淡，但纳斯达克却走出了一段单边主升浪。被压制的是那些依赖借贷、缺乏定价权的传统行业和中小盘公司，但现金流充沛、成长性极强的科技巨头在加息周期里持续跑赢。

现在把SPY和QQQ的相对比率拿出来看，会发现这个比率最近已经跌破了50日均线。这个技术形态，跟1999到2000年美联储首次加息之后走出来的走势，几乎是完全一致的。历史不会简单重复，但技术结构上高度相似。所以我觉得科技股和半导体接下来大概率会全面跑赢大盘。

如果这个逻辑继续成立，接下来的操作思路应该更聚焦。传统意义上买大盘、买等权重、追求广度这套打法，在这轮加息周期里可能会持续跑输。那些现金流极其充沛、ROIC极高、对利率脱敏的头部科技和半导体公司，会持续吸走市场里大部分的增量资金。这也是为什么最近RSP、IWM这类反映市场广度的指标持续走弱，指数还是能维持强势。

历史只是参考，不能保证1999年那轮纳指最终也走向了泡沫破裂，资金极度集中既是趋势的加速器，也可能是风险的放大器。但至少在当下这个阶段，从ROIC逻辑、巨头资本开支的刚性和SPY/QQQ相对比率的技术形态这三个角度交叉验证下来，纳指跑赢标普这个判断目前看有比较扎实的支撑。接下来的仓位配置可以更倾向于向这条主线集中。

Japan has a long weekend this week, so my wife and I went hiking today.

We went to Mt. Kongo, the highest mountain in Osaka, and I think it might be my favorite mountain I’ve been to so far.

You know, I don’t think I like hiking so much because of the sense of accomplishment when I reach the summit. There’s something about it that feels deeply human to me.

I mean, we deliberately climb a mountain where there’s nothing but trees, dirt, and grass. There isn’t even a convenience store anywhere around us. If you really think about it, it’s hard to understand why we would go out of our way to do something so unnecessary.

But that’s exactly what makes it feel so human to me. Our everyday lives are full of things that are ultimately unnecessary, and I think there’s something very human about choosing to do something unnecessary just because we want to.

I feel that very strongly when I’m hiking, and I find it fascinating. It’s not quite the same as feeling like I’m escaping from everyday life. It’s difficult to explain, but I guess I just like hiking because it reminds me of what it means to be human.

By the way, there was a statue of a bull at the summit. I made a wish that it would bring us a bull market soon. 🐂📈

Knowing my own setups are only 1/2 of the game.

I can have a strong RS name, inside day, 30min pivot, 9/21EMA crossback, or Stage 1 → Stage 2 transition, but I still need to understand the environment that setup is triggering in.

If the market is chopping around, the group is getting smoked, and every breakout is going +2% before round-tripping, I’m probably not treating that trigger the same way I would when leaders are ripping, groups are moving higher together, and my own positions are paying me.

Technicals generate my ideas, but context determines how aggressively I express them.

I’m always asking what the overall market is doing, whether the group is showing RS, how the peers are behaving, and whether buyers are actually following through and holding gains. A beautiful setup with 5 headwinds is still swimming upstream.

At the same time, put that exact same setup in a leading stock, leading group + healthy environment and suddenly I have the wind at my back.

From there, I try to make the actual trade stupidly mechanical.

- where am I entering?
- where am I wrong?
- what pivot invalidates the idea?
- how much am I willing to lose if I’m wrong?

If I’m buying a 15/30min right-side curl, maybe my risk is LOD. If I’m buying against a daily support pivot, maybe losing that pivot invalidates the entire thesis. I want those answers BEFORE I click buy because 9:47 AM with a red candle flying at my face is a terrible time to discover my risk tolerance.

And getting stopped doesn’t mean the idea was “wrong forever.” That took me YEARS to understand.

Sometimes I take the paper cut, price undercuts my level, reclaims it 30 minutes later, forms another pivot, and I buy the name right back. A stop is simply the price I’m willing to pay for information...not a restraining order against ever touching the stock again.

That’s really what I’ve tried to systematize within my own trading:

Environment → groups/themes → setup → entry → risk → invalidation → feedback.

Once those pieces are defined, I don’t need to predict where the market closes, argue with someone about fundamentals, or stare at every 5min candle.

I execute my plan, let price tell me whether I’m right, and if I’m wrong, I get out quickly enough to come back tomorrow and do it all over again.

This is how I keep it stupid simple, so I hope this helps break down this concept!

Godspeed, family.

AI bubble and the Best Approach
(Update from Howard Marks)

As taken from Bloomberg's interview over the weekend.

Interviewer: 

....But I’m curious how bubblicious this environment looks to you right now.... 

Marks: 

Well, look. The main thing is, as I wrote in the last memo on the subject, Alan Greenspan used the phrase in ’97, I think it was “irrational exuberance,” and that is the definition of a bubble. 

We certainly have exuberance. 
The question is whether it’s irrational. 

And since nobody, in my opinion, can spec out exactly what it is that AI is going to be doing and with what effect and with what profitability, I don’t think anybody can say that it’s irrational, but you have to consider the possibility. 

And so when you tackle AI from an investment point of view, you have to think about how confident you are in your judgments and, like in everything else but taken to a higher power, we have to think about how important it is to us to make all the money that’s going to be made by the most aggressive people, and are we willing to take on the uncertainty which is associated with that.

My takeaway/ stance is the same as per my post last year (attached):

No All-In,
No All Cash.
Best approach is moderate position applied with selectivity and prudence.

"Since no one can say definitively whether this is a bubble, I’d advise that no one should go all-in without acknowledging that they face the risk of ruin if things go badly.  

But by the same token, no one should stay all-out and risk missing out on one of the great technological steps forward.  

A moderate position, applied with selectivity and prudence, seems like the best approach."

6 money lessons I’m learning at 22 that I hope I’m still following at 42:

I’m becoming increasingly convinced that looking rich and becoming rich require almost opposite behaviors.

I’m only 6 years into this investing/trading journey, so I’m VERY aware that I still have a ridiculous amount to learn. But the longer I do this, the more convinced I become that the hardest part about money is getting really, really good at boring sh*t.

Everyone wants to talk about the monster trade, the 10xbagger, the huge year, or the business that exploded overnight because that’s what makes a cool screenshot. Nobody gets excited talking about managing cash properly for the 47th month in a row...and I've been slowly shifting toward the latter.

Quick money goes quick for a reason!!

But that’s increasingly where I think the real game is won:

> continue to grow my income.
> keep my expenses reasonable.
> live below my means.
> invest consistently.
> protect my capital.
> avoid catastrophic mistakes, but fail a lot.
...and then repeat.

None of those things make me feel like Warren Buffett when I wake up tomorrow morning, but do them for 10-20 years, and suddenly the boring decisions start looking pretty dang exciting. Compounding is almost invisible in the beginning...that’s why most people don’t have the patience to let it work.

Trading has probably reinforced this lesson more than anything else for me because I’ve learned that making money and keeping money are 2 VERY different skills.

I can have an incredible month, but if that immediately gives me permission to double my lifestyle, oversize trades, or start treating money differently, what exactly did I accomplish? The same applies when income increases. I don’t want every raise in earning power to automatically become a raise in spending power just because I can suddenly afford another toy.

I think short-term gratification quietly wrecks a lot of people (especially youthful men).

Everyone wants to "look" wealthy before they’ve given themselves enough time to actually become wealthy.

I’d rather build quietly unseen, increase my earning power, keep investing, live below what I could afford, and let time do its job while everyone else argues about the next shortcut.

Ask me again in 20 years and I’m sure I’ll laugh at 1/2 the stuff I thought I understood at 22. But right now, 1 principle keeps getting clearer: get exceptionally good at doing boring financial things for an unreasonable amount of time.

The home runs get the screenshots...however, consistency + capital preservation are what actually build the scoreboard.

It's always good to know the difference.

Everybody wants 100%+ returns, to catch multi-month monster moves in the leaders, and to never chase extended stocks.

Oh, and somehow do all of that without ever experiencing more than a 5% drawdown—because apparently at 10%, you’re suddenly a bad trader and your system is broken.

Shocker: that’s not how it works.

If you want to position early for a market turn instead of chasing after confirmation, you’ll sometimes get chopped up during basing periods and false starts. If you want to hold leaders for monster moves, you’ll have to tolerate volatility and give back some open profits along the way.

Higher potential returns come with a price. Get your expectations straight about returns, timeframe, drawdowns, and giveback—and make sure you’re actually willing to pay the price of your system.
